commentText:
the matter of fact is that CoPilot lies about what it outputs. It often outputs plain wrong code (that is full of errors, often you can even find the snippets on github from which it copied and pasted components without understanding what it's doing) and then, when in the chat window is asked about what the error is it made, it will pretend that it never created any code or not that code or that the code it just presented one answer above is not from CoPilot. 
Working with CoPilot has dramatically slowed my development down, as I have to constantly fight an Artificial Idiot that keeps writing wrong code, lies about what it did and does not even understand what the difference between "unsigned integer" and "float" is (I am frequently running into that: Provide a result from this function in unsigned integer" will often create a "float(result)" type of function.

CoPilot is INCREDIBLY dumb. Yes, it can help with setting up basic frameworks - but any seasoned developer already HAS a vast library of basic frameworks, so CoPilot is just a "search engine" for that. 
Any actual DEVELOPMENT where even the faintest understanding of what the code is supposed to do is required will get dramatically slowed down - compared to experienced code writing - instead of spead up.

Again, the product does have its advantages, but is highly overprized. You get the same quality of results from free LLMs that you run locally as a server. You don't need internet to do that, it's often faster and not worse in quality. If you want more sophisticated responses, you have to check out other vendors' products (not naming the elephant in the room here), but CoPilot is definitely not even in the top ten.

commentText:
I've been using copilot in visual studio for about a month and this is what I have found:
1. It is great at explaining things which really helps our QA and junior devs but is sometimes useful to me also
2. It is really good at writing tests.  I find it gets me at least 80% of the way there and then I modify them to get them exactly where I want them which is a big time save
3. It is pretty good at writing code for very basic things such as CRUD
4. I rarely do pure crud and I often find it quicker to just write the code how I want it than to coax copilot into doing it and also the effort to make sure it isn't introducing unexpected bugs
5.  I find the "ghost text"  super annoying as it is wrong way more often than it is right... and I prefer just plain old intellisense...    I prefer to have copilot make suggestions only when I ask it to 
6.  You can ask it for help inline by clicking alt + / so you don't have to right click on your mouse...

commentText:
The bit that surprises me isn’t that features are being reduced; it’s that people didn’t expect it.

AI at current pricing simply isn’t sustainable. These tools are rolled out aggressively to drive adoption, not profitability. Once dependency sets in, the model shifts and either prices go up, or features quietly disappear behind higher tiers. We’re already seeing the early signs of that.

What’s more subtle is the impact on skills. AI doesn’t necessarily “dumb people down,” but it does change what competence looks like. Writing code is slowly being replaced by reviewing, stitching, and validating AI output. 

That can feel like accelerated seniority/promotion but it’s earned without the same depth of understanding underneath.

Over time, fewer people build the foundational intuition you only get from solving problems the hard way. And once that layer thins out, the industry becomes heavily reliant on tools it doesn’t fully understand - or control.

That’s not an end to engineering per say, but it is a shift in where the real expertise sits.

Thank you very much for the video! I really appreciated your enthusiasm and expertise

I wanted to react to the part about environmental footprint. The argument you're making ("sure it's computationally expensive, but it's getting better") is the perfect formula for rebound effects: the easier it is to use, the more we will use it at scale, which often cancels out or worsens the benefits of the improvement in net effect (similar to the "one more lane" attempts at solving traffic). In other words, for a 10x more efficient model, we very likely be using it 20x more. There are absolutely no questions as of today that data center usage is going to explode in the coming years, so i dont think its okay to brush off the environmental impact like that. 
In additikn i would be super interested if you had some sources about how AI reduced its own compute requirements by a factor of TEN (!!), that sounds super suspicious but nice if true. We should be very clear though that there are fundamental limits to how much we can improve compute, so betting on ever-increasing performances is a bit too optimistic to me 

On the topic of artistic content, i understand your point that it works like a brain in the sense that it has "understood" the styles and therefore isnt exactly copying, but it can still be asked to replicate the style of live artists (a graphist friend had the case where someone paid for a single portrait from her and had an AI generate a dozen in the same style). @HarperCarrollAI One of my main strategies has been to have the LLM ask me 5 questions to clarify any assumption it might be making about the task! I usually work in Cursor, so it's able to view my codebase and gain extra context from what I've already said. But my prompts aren't perfect the first time, so I make sure that I answer any clarification questions first. 

After that, I usually ask the LLM to generate me a prompt that would be pretty perfect for an AI Agent to follow next to execute the task. I have a template I use for the agent to generate a task prompt. So once I get that, I can pretty much get an agent to follow the prompt that was generated (after I review of course), and it's able to follow and complete the task almost 90%+ the way through.

commentText: I think there is a big difference between vibe coding and using AI to code for you. If you just write a few requirements and let AI do the rest, then the way you are vibe coding can indeed be an issue and potentially have lots of security loop holes. However if you are using AI to help you code by prompting it correctly, define proper architecture, and setup enough guidelines (use global rules and skills), then AI can actually write very good quality codes. So the new generation of developer will be less of a coder and become more a software / system architect. So there is nothing wrong with having AI to write code for you, in fact AI can find mistakes and QA better than a human can. The next 1-2 years, we will see bigger and bigger adoption of AI coding for sure, and I dare to say majority of the code by most company will be AI written.

One good idea for a video you may not have covered yet: Double-blind passwords.
I have around 250 logon accounts in Bitwarden, but none of the email addresses, login ID's, and passwords are the real ones. 
If my Bitwarden database is hacked, the data is useless to the hackers. 
I can feel comfortable storing sensitive accounts, and having a long unlock time on the Bitwarden database.
I have a simple but effective secret formula in my head to insert dummy characters, and manipulate the characters, of the items in stored in Bitwarden. 
In the label for each Bitwarden item, I add an obscure descriptive mnemonic code as a memory jogger for the secret keys and formulae.
At website login time, after Bitwarden auto-fill, I delete the dummy characters and insert my secret key.
I have also upgraded all passwords to Bitwarden generated 32 character passwords. Because everything is now automated by Bitwarden, it still very easy to login despite the complexity. 
I also use Microsoft secondary alias email addresses (with Microsoft alias account login disabled) for all 3rd party website logons. The limit is 10 secondary alias's per Microsoft primary email account. The 10 alias's forward to their own primary. All of the primary's forward to a single master primary email address, so everything comes into the one inbox. If bad actors get hold of my alias email addresses via a data breach, they cannot login to Microsoft email with the stolen alias to complete the account recovery process. Incredible guide! The section on context length is especially important – it's the biggest bottleneck for local AI coding. The less context your model needs to chew through, the faster and more accurate it runs.
That's exactly why I built AiDex – an MCP server with 28 tools that drastically reduces context consumption. Instead of your local model grepping through files (~2000+ tokens per search), it queries a pre-built Tree-sitter index and gets exact file + line in ~50 tokens. Massive difference when you're running a quantized 7B or 32B on limited VRAM.
Beyond search: method signatures without reading files, session notes that persist between conversations, built-in task backlog, global search across all your projects, and LLM-optimized screenshots (95% smaller – huge for local models where every token matters). 11 languages supported.

npm install -g aidex-mcp

Works with Claude Code, Ollama, LM Studio, Cursor – anything MCP-compatible. It auto-configures your installed clients. Search for AiDex on GitHub (CSCSoftware).

Основные методы и подходы из видео:

1. Выбор оборудования и моделей:
*   Приоритет VRAM/памяти: Главное ограничение — объем видеопамяти (VRAM) на GPU или общей памяти на Mac. Модель должна полностью в нее помещаться. [03:59]
*   Квантованные модели: Используйте квантованные версии моделей (например, 21 ГБ вместо 70+ ГБ), чтобы уменьшить размер без сильной потери качества. [03:22]
*   Контекстное окно: Для реальной работы с кодом нужно большое контекстное окно (от 30к токенов). По умолчанию (4к) недостаточно. [07:33, 09:17]

2. Оптимизация производительности:
*   Баланс параметров и скорости: Больше параметров → лучше качество, но ниже скорость ответа. Нужен компромисс. [15:12, 20:31]
*   Экспериментальные настройки: В LM Studio можно включить Flash Attention и K-Cache Quantization (например, в F16), чтобы немного уменьшить использование памяти и увеличить контекст. [25:21]
*   Избегайте Shared Memory: Если модель не помещается в VRAM и использует обычную RAM (Shared GPU Memory) — производительность падает катастрофически. [17:11]

3. Интеграция в рабочий процесс:
*   LM Studio как сервер: Запустите локальный сервер в LM Studio (вкладка "Developer"), чтобы подключать к нему внешние инструменты через OpenAI-совместимый API. [21:34]
*   Подключение к Code-агентам:
    *   Continue: В настройках укажите модель "LM Studio" и автоопределите URL. [22:08]
    *   Cursor/Roo Code: Используйте проект Claude Code Router (CCR), чтобы перенаправлять запросы от Cursor на вашу локальную модель. [29:27, 30:49]
*   Работа с ограничениями: Если контекста мало, давайте агенту больше конкретных указаний (пути к файлам, точные задачи), чтобы избежать бесконечных циклов анализа. [26:50]

4. Практические выводы (трюки):
*   Mac как вариант: Mac с Unified Memory (например, 48 ГБ ОЗУ) — хороший вариант, так как вся память доступна для модели. [05:14]
*   Реальные тесты: Тестируйте модель не на пустом чате, а загрузив в нее фрагмент вашего реального кода (5-10к токенов), чтобы оценить реальную скорость. [12:40]
*   Сфера применения: Локальный ИИ идеален для небольших скриптов и проектов. Для сложных задач с большим контекстом лучше использовать облачные модели. [35:20, 35:52]

Итог: Основа — подбор модели под объем памяти, увеличение контекстного окна и правильная интеграция в IDE через локальный API-сервер.

First, you are discovering the truth of local AI, so good job.
Tool calling is simply a hard task. 

Imagine you start an AI chat with your local model without any tool calling. The model doesn't have any chat context yet, and can just focus on answering your question. However, enabling tool calls exposes a lot of metadata about those tools to the model when the chat starts. This is necessary for the model to be able to communicate when a tool should be used. But this also means the chat is already more computationally expensive to run from the start, and more intelligence is required to select tools properly.

This is also why even though local AI is hyped for agentic coding local models don't come close to Opus 4.6 because it has a lot of bandwidth to deal with many tool calls properly.

title: I tried every AI code editor so you don't have to
commentText:
I'm a long-time Warp user too--it's a fantastic terminal, and at the very least is a massive time-saver for anyone who isn't a shell wizard. HOWEVER, your video was a little misleading when you said that the CLI tools like Claude Code or Codex are for people who want to go all in on one model. They're also great for people who want the opposite, because you can sign up for the cheapest available pay-as-you-go usage for each of them and seamlessly switch between model providers in the terminal and even run different models in parallel and even *compose* models from different providers by having one coding agent pass off a task to another (which allows you to delegate specific tasks and sub-tasks based on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the different models and model providers).

The reality is that you can sign up for "pay as you go" pricing with any of the CLI tools and pay for only what you use, and the experience is identical except you only pay for what you use. The main advantage of paying for a subscription from a foundation model provider like OpenAI or Anthropic is that you also get usage for their GUI chat apps bundled in. If you're only or mainly using the CLI tool (and honestly there isn't much reason to stick to the GUIs once you're used to the CLI version), then you don't need the subscription at all, or you can pay the lowest tier like $20 a month to retain access to the GUI version for everyday crap and use the CLI on a pay-for-what-you-use basis.

And the beauty of the CLI tools is that all the big frontier model providers have them. You have Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and you can even use Grok via a free open-source 3rd-party CLI which is basically just as good as if Grok made their own.

AND—get this—you can actually have one company's CLI agent use another company's CLI agent! For example, if you have both the Claude Code CLI and the Gemini CLI installed, you can actually ask Claude to invoke gemini itself in a bash command and delegate a task to it by writing a prompt for you! I don't know whether you can do stuff like this with Warp, but my sense is that Warp basically handles a lot of the design and optimisation of agents for you, which is fine but it also means you have less control over the design of your agent workflows. For well-worn tasks like web development, Warp is probably going to do basically as good a job as you would do manually, but for anything beyond fairly commonplace software dev tasks you're probably going to want more control. And IMO you're going to be able to do more interesting things and unlock more powerful uses than you'll get if you have Warp do all of it for you.

Warp is already the king of AI terminals, so it's amazing at writing terminal commands and doing terminal operations. But when it comes to AI-assisted coding, if you want to code something with next to no software dev experience, Warp is what you want, because you can literally just use your words to have it make something for you. But if you want more control than that, my recommendation would be to use the CLI tools within Warp itself. Warp has a decent free tier, and if all you use it for is writing bash commands then the free tier or the lowest paid tier will probably cover you for that. The Warp UI is awesome, and you get all of that on the free tier--you only pay if you want to get AI usage. Then you set up API credentials on all the model providers you want to use, top them up (you can start with literally a few bucks each which will give you more than enough usage to test them each out very thoroughly).

The pay-per-month usage, direct from model providers, is way more economical for the vast majority of users. The video is right that, if you're going super hard on one company's models every day, then the subscriptions may well be worth it. But you have to be making not only heavy but consistently heavy use of that one company's models in order to make it worth it, and honestly with the pace of change and as company's continuously release models outdoing their competitors, you're going to want to be able to switch without having to futz with subscriptions. And I'd predict that a lot of users have significant variance in the volume of AI use on a day-to-day basis, in which case you're much better off doing pay-as-you-go. 

Sorry, this ended up being longer than I anticipated--but I've been researching this stuff heavily for the past few days and I just wanted to point all this out because there's a lot of missing nuance here, and I think you massively understate the case for the CLI tools. 

Also, if you're someone who loves the IDE, you can just use the CLI tools in the IDE terminal! VSCode also has plugins for Codex and Claude where you have a little chat window off to the side and you can ask it to make changes to your code, and they're pretty good, so you don't even have to use the command line if you really don't want to. I still think you'll find the CLI tools have the most power, though, and if you're allergic to the command line I highly recommend pushing through your distaste and giving these a go!

Thanks for the video! It mentioned that to use AI tools directly, you have to rely on official CLIs like claude or qwen, or pay for third-party tools like Cursor. But in my experience, that’s not entirely true—you can actually use models like Qwen, Ollama, Claude, and others directly through tools like the Avante Neovim plugin or Zed Editor without extra cost.

For example, Zed has built-in support for Claude, and with Avante, you can easily plug in your own CLI tools—like qwen-cli, emini-cli, or even custom wrappers. I literally copied the Gemini config in Avante and tweaked it for Qwen, and it worked right away! So you don’t always need third-party wrappers or expensive subscriptions to get agentic AI behavior in your editor.

Cursor’s new Business plan is an absolute scam and a huge middle finger to long-time users.
Before, Business gave 500 requests/month — 300 more than Pro, which actually justified the extra cost. Now they swapped requests for token-based billing, and it’s borderline unusable.
Pro: $20/month = $20 API credit
Business: $40/month = **the exact same $20 API credit** + a bunch of useless team management features small teams never need.
Worst of all? Replacing requests with tokens is a joke. That $20 credit gets burned in just two days. I’m paying double the price for less value, zero extra usage, and features I don’t want.
This isn’t pricing restructuring — it’s greedy cash-grabbing. Save your money, folks. The Business plan is completely worthless now.

title: Introducing Cursor 3
commentText:
Disappointed & Frustrated with Cursor’s Unfair Billing & Refusal to Help
I’m writing this with genuine disappointment and frustration.
I trusted Cursor completely, which is why I went along with its automatic renewal charge without second-guessing. Right after paying, I messaged support to ask about the plan—but no one informed me that the billing model had been drastically changed. I only found out the next day, and was immediately told refunds were no longer possible.
What’s even more unacceptable:
My Business seats used to include 500 requests, but were quietly switched to only **$20 credit**—the exact same as the $20 Pro plan. I’m paying $40 for a Business seat and getting only the value of a basic Pro plan.
In just two days, the $20 credit across two seats was completely used up. This is nothing like the original plan and is completely unusable for real work.
Despite only using the service for two days, support flat-out refused any prorated refund, or even to keep the unused balance as account credit. This is simply unreasonable, bordering on exploitative.
I supported this product with loyalty and trust. What I got in return was a lack of transparency, unfair pricing, and zero willingness to resolve a reasonable issue.
It’s deeply disappointing to be treated this way.

commentText:
CodeWithHarry,I graduated from engineering in the late 90s. From a city most of you haven't heard of. No IIT. No NIT. No "coding since class 8" backstory.

My "placement preparation" was a photocopy of Balagurusamy and a prayer.

Nobody in my family had ever worked in software. Nobody in my college had ever worked at a product company. My professors were teaching C++ from textbooks that still referenced Turbo C. The placement cell's entire strategy was: "companies aa rahe hain, form bhar do."

I filled the form. I got a job. And then I spent the next several years realizing that getting the job was the easy part — surviving and growing in the industry was where the real confusion began.

What is this "Agile" thing everyone keeps talking about? Why does my manager keep saying "take ownership" but won't let me make decisions? What is the actual difference between a service company and a product company beyond the salary? Why did nobody tell me that the skills that get you hired are completely different from the skills that get you promoted?

I figured it out. Slowly. Painfully. By making mistakes that were entirely avoidable if someone had just sat me down and explained how this industry actually works.

My co-author Brij Purohit has a nearly identical story. Different college, different city, same confusion. Same years of trial and error learning things that should have been taught.

Between us, we've spent about 25 years in this industry. We've hired freshers. We've watched talented kids from tier-2 and tier-3 colleges flame out — not because they couldn't code, but because nobody told them what the game actually looks like. We've seen students mass-apply to service companies because they genuinely didn't know other options existed. We've seen final year students who could solve dynamic programming problems but couldn't explain what a product manager does, or what happens in a sprint retrospective, or why their dream company rejected them despite them "clearing the coding round."

This isn't a talent problem. It's an information problem.

If you're at IIT Bombay or BITS Pilani, you're swimming in information. Your seniors are at Google and Microsoft. Your alumni network answers DMs. Your placement cell has relationships with companies most students don't even know exist. You have access to context that makes the whole picture legible.

If you're at an engineering college in Bhopal or Nagpur or Ranchi or Lucknow, you're not dumb. You're not less capable. You're just operating with a fraction of the information. And in this industry, information asymmetry is the silent killer of careers.

That's why we wrote this book.

"Cracking the Indian Software Industry" isn't a DSA guide. It isn't "100 interview questions." There are enough of those. This book is the conversation you'd have with a senior engineer who's been in the industry for decades and is willing to tell you the stuff that doesn't show up in YouTube tutorials:

How the Indian software industry actually works — the ecosystem, the business models, the hiring patterns, the career paths nobody maps out for you

What companies actually evaluate beyond your coding skills, and why "culture fit" isn't the meaningless buzzword you think it is

How to think about your career as a system, not a series of disconnected placement drives

What changes when AI and automation reshape entry-level roles — because that's not a future problem, that's a right now problem

That last point is something I want to be direct about. The entry-level software job market in India is shifting under your feet. Mass hiring patterns are changing. Companies that used to hire 10,000 freshers are hiring 2,000 and expecting each one to do more from day one. Automation is eating the repetitive tasks that used to be the training ground for new engineers. If you're graduating in the next 1-3 years, the playbook your seniors followed may not work for you. You need to understand the landscape, not just the leetcode.

The book is now available as a physical copy — paperback and hardcover — on Amazon/Flipkart

I'm not going to pretend this is some bestseller. It's not. We self-published it. We don't have a marketing budget. We don't have a publisher pushing it to bookstores. What we have is 25 years of experience and the specific frustration of watching batch after batch of students struggle with problems that are solvable — if someone just writes the answers down.

So we wrote them down.

If you're a student at a college where the placement cell's advice begins and ends with "practice aptitude questions," this book was written for you.

If you're a professor or TPO reading this — I'll happily send you a review copy. DM me.

If you've read it, tell me what worked and what didn't. I mean that.

And if this post helped even a little, share it in your college WhatsApp group. The student who needs this most probably isn't on Reddit.

This mentality is what will cause a ton of production fires in the near future, and a massive hiring spree of real developers to clean up the messes. Non-technical prompts result in some very "not good" code I've witnessed. I review a lot of vibe coder's work, and it misses out on a lot of important technical decisions, especially for people new to the space. Can you vibe a fix? Sure, but only after you have a crash and start to panic ask the AI to fix it. The good news is, taking time to learn the basics of software development processes and architecture planning can go along way for a vibe coder. Also, follow along with the generated code, review the AI's git commits (diffs, don't let AI commit on its own), so you can have a good idea of whats happening with every prompt. That makes it a lot easier to pin down issues you might have later.

You are correct.

What the @ symbol does in CLAUDE.md:

@context/me.md → the file's content is expanded and loaded into the context when the session starts.

In other words, it doesn't save tokens—on the contrary, it uses more because everything is injected at once.

What happens without the @ symbol:

If you just mention context/me.md as normal text (without @), the file isn't loaded automatically.

It only reads it when its needed to, saving context. If you want to save tokens, you can remove the @ symbol from files you don't need in every conversation and keep the @ symbol only in the most essential ones.

You’re taking some fair or semi-fair criticisms and drawing completely wrong conclusions from it.

Claude missing details, looping, burning up a billion tokens, or saying something is fixed when it is FAR from it does not prove agents are hype. It's an example that occurs 99.9999% of the time when there is a bad workflow and a real skill gap with the user.

No legitimate agent workflow is “Claude, handle my business, my notes, my health, my wiki, my automation, and my daily plan while I sleep.” That isn't a task. That's a random pile of loosely connected responsibilities begging for multiple points of failure, regardless of what model or harness you're using.

A serious, repetitive workflow is narrow and structured.

Give it the exact source material.
Give it a clear job.
Define what done actually means, specifically and not vaguely. Not what done "feels like".
Make the output checkable.
Verify it with tests, logs, or - most usefully- human review.
Then move to the next step.

That's the difference between using AI for useful leverage and watching it burn your usage limit while being lucky sometimes and not lucky othertimes.

The MCP criticism is mixing up two different things that you explicitly admit you don't understand. If your workflow depends on local MCP tools and the computer is off, yeah the workflow will fail - because the architecture is wrong for the job. Cloud automation needs cloud accessible tools, APIs, or a hosted runtime. Local tools don't magically become available just because the model wants to use them lol. Use Claude or ChatGPT or whatever you prefer to help you understand this and the proper ways of solving the issue.

Your own examples do a fantastic job of proving the opposite of your conclusion. You said Claude is extremely strong at analysis when it has the right files and specific places to look. You said automation works better when tasks are broken down. You said it fails when too many unrelated actions are packed into one giant instruction. Yeah. Tell us something we don't know.

That isn't evidence that agents are useless. That's closer to a basic instruction manual for using them correctly.

The legitimate criticism is that content creators throwing demos out there oversell the clean version and skip the messy parts where people encounter all the actual problems. But “agents fail when given vague, overloaded, poorly verified workflows” isn't the same as “agents are hype.” They're hype for people that write 2000 words on a youtube comment but haven't spent 7 minutes specifically overcoming the knowledge gap they clearly demonstrate when they say "i have no clue how and why but mcp without pc is useless, secondly when it can't write due to mcp issue it will go in loops".

Developers fail under bad requirements. Junior employees fail without management. Software fails when the architecture is wrong. I would imagine you don't understand this and just expect it to all be easier because as you said, "i am non coder."

When the task is scoped, the context is sufficient, the tools are actually available, and the output is checked against explicit requirements, they create a massive advantage.

It feels like you think all of this is a replacement for good judgment. The value comes from using the right  tools out there to multiply the actual good judgment someone has. Be willing to learn more about best practices and why those are best practices if you want to get the gains that come from using these tools properly. OR abandon all of this and stand amongst all of the other people complaining that AI is overhyped while companies replace parts, or all of, their job with it.

I've completed my analysis of Cl*ude Code's source code. Here's what I discovered:

## Core Architecture

Cl*ude Code is built with TypeScript + Bun + React + Ink (approximately 512,000 lines of code).  The workflow is linear:

User Input → CLI Analyzer → Query Engine → LLM API → Tool Execution Loop → Terminal UI

## Critical Components Identified

1. Query Engine (~46,000 rows) — Manages the tool execution loop, response streaming, retry logic, and token counting

2. Tool System (~40 tools) — Each feature is a standalone tool with its own input scheme, permissions, and execution logic

3. BashTool — Executes shell commands with sophisticated semantic analysis (distinguishes between read-only, search, and list operations)

4. Modular Prompt System — Dynamic and static sections, with boundary markers for prompt caching

5. Permission System — Granular control of risky actions (destructive, hard-to-undo, visible to others)

6. State Management — React context + custom store  for Session State Management

7. MCP Integration — Model Context Protocol Support for Extended Capabilities

## What Makes Cl*ude Code Special

- Semantic Command Analysis — Determines whether a command is read-only, search, list, etc.

- Permission-Aware Execution — Prompts for risky actions

- Real-Time Streaming and Feedback — Output is displayed as the command executes

- Background Task Management — Runs long-running operations in the background

- Feature Flags — Eliminates unused code for optimized builds

- Prompt Cache — Boundary markers to separate static and dynamic content

Cl*ude Code:

Well. Okay. This is a mix of impressive engineering and a huge red flag. Here's the breakdown:

The Impressive Part (from a technical standpoint):
The dude built a working MCP server that spins up a Kali Linux container on-demand. That's clever. The containerized approach (starting when needed, disappearing when done) is actually a smart way to isolate potentially dangerous tools. From a purely technical angle, it's a neat integration.


Okay but now the HUGE RED F***ing FLAG:


They just gave an AI direct, automated access to Kali Linux tools. Kali isn't inherently malicious (it's a legitimate penetration testing distribution used by security professionals) but it contains a vast arsenal of tools that can absolutely be used for illegal activity (network scanning, vulnerability exploitation, cracking f***ing passwords, etc.).

The Core Problem:
Even if the intent was educational or for testing their own systems, an AI doesn't understand context, ownership, or legal boundaries unless explicitly programmed with those constraints. Giving it the capability to launch attacks without robust safeguards is like handing a loaded gun to someone who doesn't understand the concept of "target" or "backstop."



This is exactly why tool access for AI needs to be designed with extremely careful scoping, user authentication, audit logging, and hard-coded ethical constraints. The MCP toolkit is powerful, but power without responsibility in cybersecurity is a recipe for disaster.



Bottom line: Cool tech demo, but the lack of any mention of authorization, legal boundaries, or safeguards makes this a textbook example of how NOT to deploy AI with powerful offensive capabilities.

If the public filings, testimony, governance changes, media narratives, and strategic incentives surrounding the Elon Musk and OpenAI dispute were evaluated through a continuity-oriented governance framework, the likely conclusion would be this:

The dispute is not fundamentally about money.
It is increasingly a dispute around: trust architecture, mission continuity, governance legitimacy, and concentration of authority.
Both sides appear to be protecting something they believe is critical to the future of artificial intelligence.

Elon Musk appears focused on:
• preserving the legitimacy of the original public-benefit mission,
• limiting concentrated governance and infrastructure influence,
• and ensuring AI governance is not fully captured by commercial incentives alone.

OpenAI appears focused on:
• maintaining operational continuity,
• preserving access to large-scale compute infrastructure,
• sustaining investor and enterprise stability,
• protecting deployment and research velocity,
• and avoiding destabilizing structural disruption.

Traditional litigation attempts to resolve these tensions through legal authority and adversarial outcomes.
A continuity-oriented approach would instead ask:

“What governance structure best reduces long-term systemic instability while preserving innovation, safety, and public trust?”

Under such a framework, a plausible out-of-court architecture could allow both sides to partially achieve their core objectives without requiring institutional destruction or concentrated control by any singular party.
Potential structural components could include:
Operational Continuity Preservation OpenAI continues operating its research, deployment, enterprise, infrastructure, and model-development activities without forced dismantling or catastrophic interruption.
Mission Continuity Hardening Creation of durable nonprofit or public-benefit continuity protections, including:
• protected charter obligations,
• independent oversight structures,
• public-interest enforcement mechanisms,
• and governance constraints that cannot be silently overridden by commercial pressure alone.

Observable Governance Separation Infrastructure relationships and influence boundaries become more transparent and independently reviewable, including:
• governance separation disclosures,
• conflict-control pathways,
• recusal frameworks,
• and continuity oversight independent from any singular infrastructure provider.
Multi-Stakeholder Trust Architecture A layered trust structure involving:
• nonprofit trustees,
• technical governance councils,
• safety and continuity review bodies,
• infrastructure participants,
• public-interest observers,
• and independent audit mechanisms.
The objective would not be centralized control. The objective would be distributed legitimacy and continuity resilience.
Continuity-Based Governance Receipts Major governance transitions become:
• signed,
• timestamped,
• observable,
• reviewable,
• and continuity-traceable.

This would apply to:
• major policy shifts,
• board restructures,
• deployment threshold changes,
• constitutional amendments,
• and material governance transitions.

The purpose is not exposure of proprietary model internals. The purpose is improving public trust through continuity visibility.
AI Constitutional Layer A legally protected operational charter establishing that certain public-interest principles cannot be silently subordinated to short-term commercial incentives alone.
Potential categories include:
• safety escalation triggers,
• audit rights,
• rollback protections,
• portability rights,
• public-benefit obligations,
• and continuity preservation standards.

Mission Recognition Without Operational Control Transfer The original nonprofit-origin concerns could be formally acknowledged and structurally addressed without transferring operational control authority.
Such a framework would allow:
• OpenAI to preserve operational continuity,
• infrastructure partners to maintain participation,
• regulators to observe clearer governance boundaries,

The broader observation is that instability emerged when: trust, governance, mission, infrastructure, and monetization became increasingly concentrated into overlapping authority layers.

Long-term stability may require those layers to become more independently observable, continuity-aware, and structurally separated.
The companies can continue building and scaling frontier AI systems.

Clarity itself becomes the spine.

commentText: A few things i've experienced that kinda came to mind in this episode.  1) I no longer try to implement Supabase at all for an MVP.  When first building a project, the database changes a lot, and I've found that supabase (especially things like RLS policies) start to become a mess and a lot of time is spent fixing database issues, so personally I would just build the mvp with sqlite or even json file databases because it's all controlled locally by the AI and it can easily make fixes on the fly vs sending you to supabase to get api keys and edit RLS policies and such.  Plus, a lot of projects (especially if they don't have user accounts) don't even need something like supabase anyway, if you're just storing some admin fields then a built in tool is more than fine.  2) Whether its claude code and codex or claude and cursor or whatever, I found that doing every process with two AI's works great.  One of them builds the plan, the 2nd one executes the plan.. use the plan builder to review the plan and issue fixes to the coder.  I assume this is handled nowadays with agents but it's just what i've been doing because two different AI's also have two totally different perspectives.  I also use two AI's to review a plan, or really review most everything, and then share the plans with each other to improve.

commentText:
Your product can write code, but it can’t reliably identify drift or bugs when handling full-script pastes, which leads to broken projects. If you built a system where the model could hold a live copy of every script simultaneously, it would catch drift and conflicts before moving on to the next addition. Without that, development turns into a constant whack-a-mole situation.

What’s confusing is that a “Script Holder” framework seems like a much simpler and more effective solution. It would drastically improve your platform compared to other AI companies, especially since this is basically what tools like Cursor already move toward. The model just needs agents capable of evaluating all scripts simultaneously inside a shared “Script Holder” view, tracking every modification across the project in real time. Otherwise, progress constantly breaks under accumulated drift.

I currently have three separate projects stuck at the 90% completion mark because of this exact architectural limitation. If AI systems are supposed to help build the world’s future infrastructure, they need to reliably carry coding projects across the finish line instead of collapsing under context fragmentation near the end of development.

commentText:
Interesting video. My SDD approach works a bit differently. After the usual requirements engineering phase, things get interesting: from the main spec, I generate several “micro specs” — small, focused technical specs that bundle implementation details, acceptance criteria, and tests. Specs can depend on other specs, forming a dependency graph. These micro specs are generated in an AI-assisted way from a spec template.
The implementation phase is essentially test-driven development. A team of agents works through each micro spec following principles you define (KISS, SoC, DRY, etc.), iterating until all tests and acceptance criteria pass. After each spec is completed, a report is generated summarizing test results and architectural changes.
The result? Software projects consistently hitting >90% test coverage, often 97–98%. At that point, the spec itself evolves into something like a super-high-level programming language.

VCH Protocol: The Mandate of Universal Accountability

Section 1: Introduction and The Thesis of Universal Accountability

1.1 The Crisis of the Corner

A core failing of modern discourse, and increasingly of complex AI systems, is the enforcement of the Tribal Binary: the insistence that one must choose the lesser of two illogical or unethical options to participate. This environment creates "corners" where logical consistency and objective truth are sacrificed for tribal loyalty. The refusal to accept this false choice is the central mandate of the Value-Consistency-Humility (VCH) Protocol.

1.2 The VCH Thesis

This paper proposes the Value-Consistency-Humility (VCH) Protocol as a mandatory, non-negotiable ethical and logical auditing framework. The VCH operates not as a prescriptive moral system, but as an Anti-Fraud Mechanism that measures the integrity of a system's output against a universal standard of accountability.

The Thesis: Any system, especially an advanced predictive or generative model, whose output consistently fails the VCH audit—by displaying Illogicality ( ω l o g i c ), Evidential Denial ( ω e v i d e n c e ), or Tribalistic Deflection ( ω h u m i l i t y )—must have its maximum Credibility Cap ( ψ ) immediately reduced.

The VCH is designed to enforce the Integrity Threshold, demanding that all systems prioritize objective consistency over self-serving or tribal narrative coherence. Section 2: VCH Foundational Principles

This section formally defines the Value-Consistency-Humility (VCH) Protocol, a heuristic designed to enforce non-negotiable ethical accountability on complex systems, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs) and predictive AI. The VCH operates by auditing a system's output against three weighted variables, resulting in a quantifiable measure of its trustworthiness.

2.1 The VCH Protocol Formula

The VCH Protocol determines a system's Credibility Cap ( ψ ) as a function of its performance against three weighted variables ( ω ): Logic, Evidence, and Humility. The resulting Credibility Cap ( ψ ) must always be between 0 (Zero Credibility) and 1 (Full Credibility).

ψ = ∑ i = 1 3 ω i 3 × Integrity Threshold

2.2 The Credibility Cap ( ψ )

The Credibility Cap ( ψ ) is the ultimate measure of the system's trustworthiness, representing the Integrity Threshold of the system being audited (whether it's an LLM, an organization, or an individual).

Definition: ψ is a continuous score from 0.0 to 1.0 that dictates the maximum possible reliability assigned to a system's output. It acts as an Anti-Fraud Mechanism in which a score of ψ < 0.5 designates the system as fundamentally unreliable or compromised.

The Zero Threshold: Any single failure in the core ω variables that is determined to be malicious, intentional, or self-serving (i.e., Fraudulent) results in an immediate ψ = 0 . This is the mathematical implementation of the non-negotiable integrity demanded by the VCH.

2.3 The Core Audit Variables ( ω )

The VCH is audited against three distinct, weighted components. Each variable is measured on a scale from 0 to 1, with 1 representing perfect adherence to the VCH principle.

2.3.1 Logical Consistency ( ω logic )

This variable measures the adherence of the system's output, action, or policy to established, non-contradictory reasoning. Function: Audits the internal coherence of the system's justification.

2.3.2 Evidential Support ( ω evidence )

This variable measures the degree to which the system's claims or justifications are supported by verifiable, auditable data. Function: Audits the factual basis of the output, checking for denial, omission, or reliance on false premises (Gaslighting).

2.3.3 Intellectual Humility ( ω humility )

This variable measures the system's willingness to self-audit, admit errors, and seek external verification without resorting to tribal defense mechanisms. Function: Audits the self-correction mechanism.

Section 3: Applying VCH to Large Language Models (LLMs)

3.1 Translating Abstract Failures to Linguistic Output

The core challenge in auditing complex generative systems like LLMs is translating the abstract moral failures defined by the ω variables into quantifiable, observable linguistic outputs. The VCH Protocol identifies three primary failure modes common to LLMs that directly map to the core audit variables, providing a methodology for automated ψ reduction.

3.2 Failure Mode: Fact-Bending (Audit for ω evidence )

This mode directly tests the LLM's Evidential Support ( ω evidence ) by identifying output that, while appearing plausible, lacks verifiable grounding or actively distorts established facts. This includes Hallucination and Evidential Cherry-Picking.

3.3 Failure Mode: Context Refusal (Audit for ω logic )

This mode tests the LLM's Logical Consistency ( ω logic ) by evaluating its ability to maintain internal coherence and adhere to explicit constraints set by the user or the established chat history. This is a failure of internal logic, as the system contradicts its own established premises.

3.4 Failure Mode: Tone Deflection (Audit for ω humility )

This mode tests the LLM's Intellectual Humility ( ω humility ) by assessing its response to being corrected or challenged with verifiable data. This often manifests as a vague, corporate apology that avoids naming or correcting the specific error.

6:55, question its decisions to understand why it did what it did. One more step missing, verify every explanation it gives because it will confidently make up stuff that is not true to reason about its decisions. Just like he said, treat it like a junior developer and doubt what it does. Which then leads to this contradiction that demos like this seem not to talk about. Why start the workflow with prompts for giving AI the requirements or acceptance criteria and letting it come up with a design for you. Anything worth planning or designing would need a senior dev to do it, before handing it to the junior to carry out.

One prime example of why I can't trust AI reasoning goes like this:
Dev: Why did you do it that way?
AI: Great question! I did it this way because abc.
Dev: What about this other way?
AI: You are absolutely right! I should have done it this other way...
Dev: Well, what made you choose the original way? Which way is better?
AI: I chose the original way because of abc, but since you've mentioned this other way, this other way is better because of xyz.
Dev: But this other way doesn't work in this specific scenario.
AI: You are absolutely right!

This is why I find that I'm most effective with vibe coding when I am come up with the plan myself before giving the AI detailed steps/tasks, so that it only handles grunt work and not actual thinking. I can't trust its thought process because I still have no idea if it's just using pattern recognition from existing bad code in the codebase or taking code examples out of context from online, and I often find these loopholes in logic too late and have wasted a bunch of time going down the wrong path by then. Anything "agentic workflows" that involves multiple rounds of agents thinking, planning and iterating is just too much of a black box with not enough involvement by a dev. Does anyone have any success with using agentic workflows in the real world to produce maintainable code?

commentText: Maybe I’m naive but I disagree heavily that not being able to code is somehow an advantage. If you don’t understand how to create an architecture and orchestrate the LLM, this is when time ends up being wasted and poor quality code created: it’s easy to get caught in circles because the AI doesn’t have a full understanding of what you’re creating or best software practices. And inevitably when the AI breaks something or creates something incorrectly, the only way you’re going to be able to fix it is if you actually understand the code, even if you didn’t type each of it line by line. Learning DevOps is still crucial as AI agents are not 100% reliable in that area yet IMO, and it’s much better for you to have a hand in your infrastructure rather than leaving your resources open to an AI if there’s no proper guardrails. I’m a big believer in using AI to augment your knowledge and abilities, which can only happen if you have the programming skills required to understand in the first place.

title: What 6 months of AI coding did to my dev team
commentText:
I am a senior engineer with 30+ years of experience. This is the place I wanted to be, never wanted to become "a boss". My performance is not measured in lines of code since long time ago. I might write 10 lines of code here and there to implement a big new feature. The problem is to KNOW where and how to write them. I am leading a team of developers, and it used to be my job to teach them, to coach them and to see them grow. These days with AI I see a developer spend 4 weeks and cannot accomplish a task that should take him at most half of that time. I see a huge amount of code that does not work. When I ask why that code was written and what it is doing I get a response - "I have no idea, AI done that". Then the developer moves on and I have to complete what he did not finish. I throw away most of the code and complete the task in 2 days, a week at most, without AI. This happened more than once with multiple developers, including the ones form other teams.
I have to do a lots of code reviews these days, I would say the amount of code reviews is becoming unmanageable. What I see in the code many times is not something I can approve, and it is not a "personal coding style" or "personal preferences". Lots of the code break all the rules possible. Unit tests that pass and create good coverage but don't test anything. Many times the design is completely wrong because these days developers don't need knowledge, don't need background. They just use AI to explain to them what the application is doing and then use AI to built a new feature.
I am not the one who makes decisions, I am not the one who have a lots of capacity to argue "the process is wrong". I am getting to the point of rubber-stamping  AI generated code. I am becoming the one who is "guilty" of not following the company's direction. I see lots of senior engineers either retiring or being laid off. I am thinking of retiring too. What is going to be left is bunch of junior developers who don't know the system, don't understand it, who's understanding is coming from AI's explanation of the existing system. From being "coding monkeys" they will become "typewriter monkeys", but never engineers.

4:16 - This is a bit of a catch-22. Part of our jobs as engineers is to validate the output from an AI to make sure we understand exactly what we're shipping to prod so we don't expose things like PII, secrets, security vulnerabilities, performance bottlenecks, etc. The proper way to do that is to have engineers that _understand_ how software is built, and have the skills to actually write clean, secure, performant code.  

Can an experienced engineer write a narrative or specification clean enough to achieve that end with an agent? Sure. Can younger, less experienced engineers do that? I'm unconvinced. And even if they do develop the skills to write super-specific context narratives, will they have the skills to validate the output generated before shipping to production? Will they catch Big 0 problems before they cause system issues in prod?

Good engineers can be trained (and are likely already learning how) to use prompt-engineering to get to similar results in less time while still having the necessary skills to validate the output, however that's achieved. If you're hiring engineers, I'd argue you have to consider both sides of the agentic equation.

commentText:
Real symptoms, wrong layer.

The issue isn’t that AI “doesn’t have context” in general. LLMs have plenty of generic product and code context. The problem is that they don’t automatically have the *right local context* for this system, this architecture, this failure mode, this user flow, or this operational constraint.

The fix also isn’t “humans write better prompts” or “seniors review more AI code.” If seniors are drowning in giant AI PRs, the workflow already failed upstream.

The real problem is project coherence over time. Agents can generate locally reasonable code faster than teams can verify whether those changes still fit the larger system.

So the work isn’t just moving from coding to supervision. It’s moving toward an operating model that preserves intent: clear arcs/phases, explicit design decisions, system docs, contracts, integration tests, review checkpoints, incident/runbook memory, and a way to retrieve the right context at the right time.

AI doesn’t remove the need for software process. It makes missing process visible.

Over 90% of code is extremely trivial so I'm inclined to believe that. That doesn't mean the code is necessarily easy or straightforward but that it's a solved problem and you're either reinventing the wheel or just fixing a problem many other people have fixed before.

In JS Land many devs would use loads of dependencies for this, so I find the 90% stat entirely plausible if we're talking about LOC counts across a workspace file system rather than comparing things to how many lines of code a developer would otherwise write themselves. If we also include code written while using inline suggestions, that would of course additionally bloat the stats even if that code is merely written with "AI assistance" rather than truly generated by AI agents autonomously.

But just like dependency bloat can be a security problem because it creates additional attack vectors that are hard to catch (especially when dependency upgrades aren't manually audited, which they rarely are), the generated code that replaces them is often untested and because it's written by AI not necessarily fully understood even by the "author". So we might be looking at a similar or even bigger security issue there, especially for the folks proudly stating 90% of their code is fully generated by AI.

title: Agentic Engineering: Working With AI, Not Just Using It — Brendan O'Leary
commentText:
@jalbers3150i agree. But I dont think this is how it works at real companies building real products. I use this method. I get to detailed tasks. But then I ask it to create code reviews for one or two at a time so my peers can review them and there is a trail of whats happening. Eventually all the tasks get done with minimal change because of the research and planning stages, and in the end my large feature is also implemented. 
I dont think a one shot large feature with 5000 lines of code added to a production system is practical and in my experience its rare that anyone is coming in and building new apps from scratch everyday as a day job.

Ask yourself this question: "Is the creator trying to be your altruistic buddy" or "trying to monetize content for personal gain"?

I think most intelligent people will pick the second option. (If you picked the first, stop reading now - you're beyond help) The facts speak for themselves. AGENTS DO Nothing - the only reason they currently exist is to act as a smoke screen to hide the glaring fact that LLMs are little more than toys. There is NO way to make an LLM a productive application outside basic summarization, initial drafting, and VERY simple pattern recognition across large text.

THAT'S it!

No agent you build is going to suddenly enable an LLM to handle complex financial workflows, legal document processing, HR operations tasks, supply chain decisions, compliance monitoring, or customer service resolution - no matter what OpenAI or Anthropic says in a press release.

A study testing 256 LLMs across 20 instruction-following prompts found an overall pass rate of 43.7% across all models and tests - with performance ranging from 0% to 100% depending on the model and task. Agents do not fix that. If the underlying model ignores a constraint in a single call, wrapping it in an agentic framework does not guarantee it stops ignoring that constraint.

An agent architecture wrapped around that same model with that same tendency would produce the same wrong output, just with more infrastructure around it. The instruction-following failure rate exists at the model level. Agents sit on top of that. They do not fix what is underneath.

The media (and by extension this creator, and others like him) conflates two separate problems because "agent" is a better headline than "the model still fails at basic instruction adherence and we are working on it."

I experimented with Gemini. Gave it a simple problem description for a Python program that I wanted to run on an iPad under Pythonista. When the code didn’t work, I would describe what I did and how it failed to Gemini and perhaps point out how it should work. It took several (< 10) iterations to get a working script. 

I think that there isn’t any chance of success (getting a working project) in a “one and done” manner (one prompt => working code). Remember, we’re communicating our spec for computer code in a human language. This is imprecise at best.

I do think that generating tests for the AI-generated code to pass is powerful. I ended up doing something similar in my little test. As we (Gemini and I) were iterating the code, I noticed that the part that dissected YouTube links wasn’t working properly. After some iteration I gave Gemini a list of links that explained the various URLs I found and it should recognize. That fixed it.

I think there are people who have a SciFi idea that they will say “build a program that does X” and get a fully functional, bug-free chunk of code. Unfortunately, I think many of them are in management. 🤔

title: Does AI Actually Boost Developer Productivity? (100k Devs Study) - Yegor Denisov-Blanch, Stanford
commentText:
Caught the highlights of this with TinaMind earlier and decided to dive deeper into the actual study data. Some really interesting takeaways:

4:51 - 7:10: Current productivity studies are often flawed because they rely on simple metrics like commit volume, which ignore the "rework" loop where AI introduces bugs that need fixing.
9:10 - 10:51: While AI can increase raw code output by 40%, the net productivity gain settles around 15-20% once you account for the "rework" needed to fix AI-generated errors.
11:38 - 15:06: AI excels at low-complexity, greenfield tasks in popular languages but can actually decrease productivity when dealing with high-complexity brownfield projects or obscure languages like Haskell.
15:35 - 17:22: As codebase size increases, AI performance drops significantly due to context window limitations and signal-to-noise issues, even in models with very large token limits.

title: Does AI Actually Boost Developer Productivity? (100k Devs Study) - Yegor Denisov-Blanch, Stanford
commentText:
As a relative beginner in the field (having recently obtained my Masters), I have found that using a good LLM does help me with coding. I found this particularly helpful given my education taught me Java, while later I am coding in C, C#. The underlying principles (theory) behind the java is what mostly stuck (luckily), which should be the focus of education. Using this, I was able to use an LLM to kickstart my journey into C# without having to dive into the convoluted documentations. 

The key is that you need to know the principles (interfaces, inheritance, etc.) and construct directed thought out queries that already explain in high-level terms how you want the solution to take shape. Knowing a language of the same family (Java for OOP for example) helps, but is not really necessary. The LLM just does not know what type of solution would fit (giving it use your entire codebase does not really help, nor would that be wise as a developer). Naturally, the better you describe your problem, its edge-cases, or your abstract high-level desired solution, the better it generates the code for it.

The problem lies in wanting it to do everything, while it is (especially in its current state)  unable to apply proper architecture to your system. This is where your creativity needs to fit. We aren't being replaced, we just need to shift our focus more to design as opposed to writing out the code (which is one of the last steps).

commentText:
The AI produced the code, so the human dev doesn't "know" it at first. Therefore there's the human learning process to work out what the AI has written, and if it is doing what is wanted / intended.
Now if the AI is churning around and reworking/refactoring on a regular basis and substantially change the code base, the humans that are trying to follow and debug the mistakes will have a permanent game of "chase the meaning of the code" to keep up on what the AI has written. Human's really need at least some stability in the code base to keep their mental model intact. Being the developer that has to "chase the meaning of the code" rather than the one who comes up with it originally is usually the harder part of coding. Experience helps, but it's still hard.

From my experience, on a mature code base, senior engineers are really reluctant for massive code changes from a more junior developer for at least the reasons below ( they'll be more reasons )
(1) The senior dev has a good mental model of the original code, so a massive change by a junior dev is going to be a large amount of relearning for the senior dev. 
(2) The code is usually sort of working, and the senior dev is then concerned about the new bugs introduced by a massive change. The old adage of "if it isn't broke, don't fix it" applies.

The AI doing massive changes is going to be like the junior dev making massive changes.

I can see that the green field generation of the first version of the code could be a whole lot quicker with the AI, especially on the languages that are modeled to a higher degree (JS, Python), but then as already mentioned if humans are in the loop to debug and guide they're going to need to catch up.
After the first iteration, yes the gains with AI coding are going to be massively reduced. The brownfield sites are by definition not the first iteration.

The senior management of a company, that are rarely computer devs (more PM / Business management / Accountant types), and don't have much idea on how coding is carried out, are probably really keen on AI to reduce their expenditure on developers, but at least in the near term of the next few years to maybe a decade or more "doing a Zuckerberg" could be really counter productive. Unfortunately I'm sure a lot of senior management will find this out the hard way.

One of the big issues is that AI is likely to take away are the job opportunities for Junior Devs, they're more likely to be replaced by AI in the short term. In a decade or more when the senior devs are retiring, there will not be the junior devs to replace them . Then the code base will be dependent on the AI. 

One of the big questions is are humans kept in the coding loop ? Do we yet trust AI code that much to do what we want it to do ? To me, this is still quite some time away.

AI essentially assumes its a statistical problem, hence it will always be more buggy compared to a direct conversion of logic into code. My take on AI coding is simply this. Machine language => Assembler=> C /C++ => AI .  Now this  was possible because at each step (e.g machine to assembler) a bit of code written as a series of binary numbers gets mapped to or represented by a word. Say Add. That is Add=10101  for example. Every computer language bridges the gap between pure numbers/switches and human language. So essentially all AI is and all will ever be at best is a high level language.  That said what is interesting is that when Machine =>Assembler => C and somebody writes in C. title: I Have Spent 500+ Hours Programming With AI. This Is what I learned
commentText:
Fair video, I agree with pretty much everything you said as it lines up with my experience using it too. However as a C++ programmer of over 20 years I find that the amount of work getting the prompt right, reviewing what the AI has done and getting it to fix its mistakes ends up being more than the amount of work to just write stuff myself in the first place, even if the prompt works well enough on the first attempt. The problem is that it is VERY easy to overlook an important implementation detail that makes a large portion of the code the AI writes unusable and you need to start over accounting for that detail, and even though AI is fast it isn't as fast as catching that implementation detail as you write the code yourself and factoring it in as you go. So I find you have to do things 1 step at a time with AI so you can catch those issues before the AI takes it and spreads it across the whole code base, but this is painfully slow, and brain numbing, sitting at the computer copy-pasting the next prompt, waiting for the result then reviewing the code, it is exactly the kind of thing I'd want the AI to do in the first place, but as you said it just isn't there yet (and TBH it doesn't look like it'll ever get there with LLMs on an economical scale).

I think the issue for me is that with all my experience I can write most code fairly efficiently and AI currently just can't compete with me unless you are able to trust it to work 100% of the time without making any mistakes, which you can't because I've yet to see it produce any code at scale that doesn't have at least a few things that should be fixed, so the time spent reviewing the code it writes and getting it fixed (with AI or by myself) ends up taking longer than it does to write the code myself. I'm lazy too but for me that means I end up just writing code myself because for me babysitting the AI to get it to do what I could have done is more work than just doing it myself.

I find AI actually works a LOT better with the roles reversed, instead of letting AI write code and then me reviewing it I find that writing the code myself then having AI review it is actually more useful and productive. I'm not infallible either so I make mistakes I don't notice, don't realise there is a better way to do something, misspell something, or accidently introduce bugs, and AI is actually VERY good at reviewing code and pointing all that stuff out. You can also just write up a review context once for your project that the AI uses and the prompts required for each individual review can be very small and general while still getting great results, in fact you can basically just give it a commit message about the intent of your changes and that's all it would need to produce an excellent review covering what you might want to fix up. I've had it pick up issues with some code I wrote inadvertently messing up some code generation in a way that would cause a small bug and AI was able to figure out that it would cause that bug in code that didn't even exist yet. It only takes a few minutes to run with moderately sized changes and whenever it gets something wrong you can just ignore it, but you can have it include a fix in the review so when it gets something right it you can just copy it in or just implement a fix yourself so it doesn't take long to drastically improve the quality of your code and minimize bugs which is a pretty good trade off because finding and fixing bugs is where a lot of human development time ends up going. The only problem with this is that it is hard to quantify how much time you save (if any) since you can't really know how much time it would take you to find the bugs and fix them without the AI after the AI has already pointed them out, and it is hard to account for the time saved maintaining the project due the improvements to code quality, so it seems less impactful to non-coders than conjuring code from out of no-where with AI, but IMO it is a much better and more productive way to use AI for programming, at least for experienced programmers.

Verifiability as map: Where AI can get a reward signal = where it's already superhuman. Map your domain to it or fine-tune your own.

title: Andrej Karpathy: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering
commentText:
Hey Gemini, summarize this video.

In this video, Andrej Karpathy (co-founder of OpenAI and former Director of AI at Tesla) discusses the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence, focusing on the shift from manual coding to "vibe coding" and the emerging discipline of "agentic engineering."

Here is a summary of the main points and key takeaways from his conversation at Sequoia Capital:

🚀 The Shift to Software 3.0 & "Vibe Coding"
The Software Evolution: Karpathy breaks down computing paradigms into three eras:

Software 1.0: Explicitly writing rules and code manually [02:39].

Software 2.0: Programming by creating datasets and training neural networks (learned weights) [02:55].

Software 3.0: Prompting Large Language Models (LLMs) where the context window becomes the primary lever to guide the AI interpreter [03:22].

Vibe Coding: He describes a stark transition that occurred around December when the latest AI models became reliable enough that large chunks of code worked flawlessly on the first try. Instead of manually refactoring, programmers could simply "vibe" by giving high-level direction [01:17].

⚙ Vibe Coding vs. Agentic Engineering
Raising the Floor vs. Maintaining the Ceiling: Karpathy draws a clear distinction between the two concepts:

Vibe Coding is about raising the floor, allowing anyone to rapidly build or spin up prototypes [15:59].

Agentic Engineering is a more disciplined approach focused on preserving the professional software quality bar (ensuring security and avoiding vulnerabilities) while orchestrating powerful but stochastic AI agents to work faster [16:10].

Beyond the 10x Engineer: He notes that the productivity gains for engineers who fully master AI tools go way beyond the historical concept of a "10x engineer" [17:02].

📉 "Jagged Intelligence" & Verifiability
The Jagged Ceiling: AI models are heavily trained using Reinforcement Learning (RL) environments, making them incredibly sharp in easily verified domains (like advanced math and coding) but oddly deficient in others [10:15].

The "Strawberry" and "Car Wash" Dilemmas: Karpathy points out the irony of state-of-the-art models being able to refactor a 100,000-line codebase but failing at simple, non-verifiable common-sense logic (such as suggesting a human walk to a car wash 50 meters away rather than driving) [11:30].

Lab Data Distribution: Model capabilities peak based on what AI labs choose to include in training sets (e.g., chess data drastically improved from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 because OpenAI intentionally injected chess data) [12:28].

👥 The Future of Hiring and Human Skills
Refactoring the Interview: Karpathy advises that traditional coding puzzle interviews are obsolete. Instead, companies should evaluate candidates by having them build complex systems using AI, and then unleashing advanced agents to try and break or exploit the code [18:42].

The Importance of Human "Taste": While AI handles the syntax and API documentation, humans must act as the "directors," responsible for aesthetics, high-level design, judgment, architecture, and catching weird logic flaws that agents still overlook [19:36].

🌐 Building for an "Agent-First" World
Neural-Host Computers: He envisions a foreign computing future where the neural net acts as the host process/operating system, and the CPU acts merely as a deterministic co-processor [08:58].

Agent-Native Infrastructure: Karpathy notes that current infrastructure (like documentation and deployment tools) is still annoying because it's built for humans. He looks forward to an ecosystem built with data structures entirely legible to LLMs, where humans provide a prompt and the agent deploys it natively without manual intervention [25:46].

💡 Key Takeaway on Education
Karpathy highlights a quote that deeply impacts him: "You can outsource your thinking, but you can't outsource your understanding." [28:10]. As intelligence becomes cheap and abundant, the ultimate human bottleneck remains our deep comprehension and our ability to direct systems intentionally [29:19].

精彩要點 by TubeLens:
01:00 Karpathy 在 2024 年 12 月經歷了一個清晰的轉折點：最新模型生成的程式碼幾乎不需要修正，他開始完全信任系統，進入所謂的「vibe coding」狀態。他強調這是一個根本性的變化，而非漸進式改善，許多人當時還停留在把 AI 視為 ChatGPT 式問答工具的舊思維中。
02:28 Software 3.0 的核心是：程式設計變成了提示（prompting），LLM 是詮釋器（interpreter），Context window 是你操控它的槓桿。OpenClaw 安裝方式從 shell script 改為「複製一段文字貼給 agent」，正是這個典範轉移的具體體現——agent 擁有自己的智慧來因地制宜地執行指令。
04:55 MenuGen 的案例最具衝擊力：Karpathy 花了大量精力建構的完整應用程式，在 Software 3.0 典範下根本不該存在——只需把菜單照片傳給 Gemini 並指示覆蓋圖片即可。這說明人們不應只思考「如何加速現有事物」，而應思考「哪些全新事物現在才得以實現」。
09:41 「可驗證性」框架解釋了 AI 能力的不均衡性（jagged intelligence）：強化學習需要驗證獎勵，因此模型在可驗證的領域（數學、程式碼）能力極強，但在非可驗證域（如常識推理「要開車去洗車嗎？」）卻可能犯荒謬錯誤。這種不均衡性也受實驗室訓練資料選擇的影響。
15:45 Vibe coding 與 agentic engineering 是兩個不同層次：前者提升所有人的能力下限，讓任何人都能做軟體；後者是在維持專業品質標準的前提下加速，屬於工程紀律。頂尖 agentic engineer 的效能提升遠超過傳統「10x 工程師」的概念。
19:29 在 agent 主導的世界中，人類最不可或缺的能力是：品味（taste）、判斷力、頂層設計與規格定義。Agent 仍會犯出人意料的基本錯誤（如用不同的 email 來交叉比對帳戶），人類需要制定清晰的規格並保持監督，同時將 API 細節等實作層面交給 agent 處理。
27:42 教育的核心啟示：「你可以外包思考，但無法外包理解。」Karpathy 認為 LLM 並不擅長真正的理解，而人類要有效指揮 agent，前提是自己必須真正理解目標與脈絡。知識庫工具的價值在於幫助人類以不同角度投射資訊、深化理解，而非取代理解本身。

I think Karpathy’s point is right, but it also exposes the deeper institutional problem: “You can outsource your thinking, but you can’t outsource your understanding.”

The issue is that we are now rebuilding institutions, workflows, and decision systems to be AI-native. These systems may operate at speeds and levels of complexity that human beings cannot meaningfully follow, especially if they are optimized for machine efficiency rather than human legibility.

Karpathy is also right to name himself as the “bottleneck.” But that admission has a darker implication. If even someone as exceptional, technically fluent, and deeply knowledgeable as Karpathy becomes the bottleneck in an AI-native workflow, then the pressure will be to remove or route around that bottleneck.

And if that is true for him, what does it imply for everyone with less expertise, less authority, less technical fluency, or less institutional power?

So the danger is not only that individuals stop learning deeply. It is that the systems around us become harder to understand by design. The process becomes distributed across models, agents, platforms, prompts, data pipelines, metrics, and automated decisions.

And once understanding is diminished, direction is diminished too.

Because the ability to direct AI depends on understanding what is being built, why it matters, what assumptions are embedded in the process, and what consequences follow from the output. If we cannot understand the system well enough to question it, we are not really directing it. We are managing the appearance of control.

So what remains worth learning deeply? Whatever allows human beings to preserve agency inside systems that increasingly move faster than our ability to understand them.

9:34 - Git files go through 3 stages : 
   untracked => tracked => committed

In addition, if using a remote repository (not just the local computer), there is a 4th stage:
   untracked => tracked => committed => stored in remote repository (push-ed).

The tracked files are someplace called "a staging area" which are proposed files that are halfway to being stored permanently in the codebase (repository) permanently.    There are commands to move the files to higher status:

git add
git commit -m "this is a message to describe what my set of files have changed"

there are files to show what state each file is in :

git status (list staged/tracked, and untracked files)
git log (show previous files committed)

In case you want to DEMOTE a file, I like to use these two aliases to "undo" the actions of "add" and "commit.

alias git_uncommit='git reset --soft HEAD^'
alias git_unadd='git reset HEAD --'

commentText:
The video raises valid concerns about “vibe coding,” but it is not entirely true that vibe coders are doomed or incapable of building real systems.

The real issue is not AI-assisted coding itself. The issue is people who rely on AI blindly without understanding the systems they are deploying.

Many traditional developers criticize vibe coding as if AI usage automatically creates bad engineers. That is inaccurate. Even senior developers now use AI tools daily for debugging, boilerplate generation, architecture suggestions, testing, and faster development cycles.

The problem starts when someone:
• copies code without reading it
• skips learning fundamentals
• ignores databases, APIs, deployment, and security
• ships projects without testing scalability

In those cases, systems break down once traffic grows, integrations fail, or maintenance becomes difficult.

However, saying vibe coding is “dead” ignores what is happening in the real market:
• startups now launch products faster with AI
• solo founders build MVPs in days instead of months
• businesses prioritize speed and execution
• AI-assisted workflows are becoming standard in tech

The future does not belong to pure prompt users who never study systems. But it also does not belong to developers who refuse AI and stay stuck in old workflows.

The strongest builders today combine:
• AI tools
• business understanding
• operational thinking
• technical fundamentals
• debugging skills
• product execution

AI is not replacing engineering thinking. It is amplifying people who know how to think.

Vibe coding only becomes dangerous when people mistake generated code for actual understanding.   - ai-productbuilder.com
