I came into system design from outside the traditional developer path, and AI helped me translate ideas into specs, workflows, routes, logic, and operating-system concepts that eventually became EAV and the broader HYBRID WAYSS ecosystem.

Vibe coding without understanding is dangerous.

I use AI for pair programming, with me leading. commentText: note that the software engineer at google said that the code is an artifact. An artifact is a generated content from a mechanism (could also be a compilation output). LLM is a probabilistic function where the domain is the probable input token in the range of all possible characters, and the output is the tokens stringed together. There is no way a probabilistic machine can map all the possible inputs to the correct output. It’s just impossible by the very nature of infinity. TLDR; LLM will never replace anything.

commentText:
Scale is important here and often forgotten about in this conversation. When it comes to building a small, simple, synchronous application where you don't need to worry too much about security or privacy, then AI will do an amazing job.

But that's not what most large scale services are. Dealing with large volumes of concurrent requests, handling race conditions, security issues, service reliability, scaling within acceptable boundaries, being able to extend with additional features without breaking existing functionality, etc, etc. these aren't the extra stuff. This IS the product.

The fallacy in these conversations is that software engineers are "coders". Coding is the easiest part of the job. It was never the bottleneck. Software engineering is a problem solving profession.

AI won't replace engineers, it will empower engineers.

But the people making decisions don't understand this, they are making hiring/firing decisions based on technology they don't understand. Breaking the pipeline of grads/junior engineers coming into the industry is going to create a major problem a few years from now.

title: The Vibe Coding Era: Why AI Won’t Replace Software Engineers
commentText:
Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending toward zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 50; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 900; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 15,000 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

I like it because I've actually been able to have success creating things in code.

This is point on. The jobs change, but they don't disappear.

It's like the fear of bookkeepers, that the computer will lead to massive reduction in bookkeepers, because the majority of their work is calculating and writing things down.
Suddenly, bookkeepers were much more efficient doing this.
But instead of less bookkeepers, we got more. Because they now were able to expand bookkeeping from "purely passive keeping" to "actively optimizing". Suddenly, the bookkeeping expanded into controlling. And companies were able to reduce stock due to active stock management. And so on. 


This is the same in basically every application of a new technology. It changes, it doesn't replace. And for 5 industrial revolutions, it always caused more employment and more productive employment.

You're really an optimist. That's nice. Unfortunately, probably not a realist. (An optimist is someone who doesn't see things as tragically as they really are 😆)

AI will in the future take over the work of many people and cause unemployment to grow enormously. The fact that this isn't the case yet is no argument whatsoever that it can't be the case in the coming years.

You say that AI's tendency to give wrong answers rather than no answer at all. Yes it is a real effect — at the moment. But this has already improved dramatically, see Anthropic. The reason for this is largely already understood and lies in flawed reward strategies during the training phases. That will soon be a thing of the past.

You say that AI makes too many mistakes to be trusted. That's why it couldn't replace people. Seriously? Then why are there so many employees who make mistakes and still don't get fired? Because making mistakes is human? 😆😆😆

Because humans make mistakes, we have tests, development processes, bureaucratic approval processes, elaborate reviews, test engineering, unit tests, integration tests, system tests, tracing, logging, quality monitoring, and so on. The fact that the coding process is error-prone has never stopped investors throughout the history of software development from hiring coders. Why should that be the case with AI coders? 

Sure, you need human oversight and control, but AI makes coding so much easier that you need fewer people to do the same work. And a brief look back at history helps too: of course automated looms require human operators and technicians, but right after the invention of the power loom, 70% of weavers lost their jobs. Two hundred years ago, 90% of the population worked in farming. Then came agricultural machinery.

In the past you had to evaluate (level 3) the sources you gathered, analyze their usage for your goal (level 4), and creatively (level 5) integrate it into your code.

In short, prompting =/= learning

title: Are Programmers Obsolete?  Will AI Replace Them?
commentText:
AI has absolutely no hope of replacing developers, but it does stand a good chance of skyrocketing demand for developers.

If AI means more people build more software, that inevitably means there will be more software-exposed firms that need to hire developers to maintain and extend that software. The fact that LLMs produce *custom code* makes that even more true: since the code LLMs are producing is not standardized into a product (like no-code platforms or SaaS products), but is rather bespoke code, once it becomes so bloated and complex that the LLM can't handle it anymore, it will require human programmers to maintain and extend.

So: 
- the productivity of software developers will go way up, because they are able to produce more software with the assistance of AI
- the demand for software engineers will go way up, because more people will have custom bespoke code in need of human maintenance and extension
- the demand for software engineers will go way up, because firms newly entering software with LLM-generated code will discover new problems and contexts that are outside of the LLM's distribution

AI gets better by saturating their training distributions. They do not show any ability to get smarter beyond their training data, or generalize creative solutions to new problems outside their training data. But software engineering, at its vanguard, has always meant developing creative ways to solve new problems with software. If AI replaced all the software developers, it would mean all forward progress in software would halt: AI would be better than anyone at solving all our current problems, but completely unequipped to solve any future problems. For AI to continue being useful, it will always have to live alongside humans: learning from our creativity and saturating the new distributions that human creativity outputs.

title: Are Programmers Obsolete?  Will AI Replace Them?
commentText: I would bet that most developers have been through at least one 'obselecense scare' already unless they are just out of school. I develop embedded systems. I used to write all the driver code myself (code that sets up clocks, controls SPI/UART, etc). Then the processor vendors started making code generators to configure the drivers. Just click some buttons and out comes the code! At first I rejected them because the code quality was bad. They improved a lot over a 5 year span. Now I use them for 80% of the driver code. They are still wasteful and slow, but they are sufficient if you just have to configure something once. And time to market is much faster. It sounds analogous to what happened long ago once developers switched from assembly to C. The compilers sucked at first, and now they are so good that in most cases its probably going to better than most people (including me). But you still might write an interrupt handler in assembly now and then.

A very interesting perspective.
However, I have to add a perspective of my own:

I worked in the tech industry as a software engineer for 25 years, when it really was complex and a lot of tech was very new and emerging (1980s - 2000s).
I no longer work as a software engineer (I'm old now and have had to accept new cohorts of fresh techies year-on-year, who need their own space and deserve the same opportunities I have enjoyed).
Nonetheless, I recall very clearly how much we engineers would work *together* on projects, face-to-face and in harmony when working to deadlines vs. market/customer demands.

Notwithstanding the obvious social and emotional support inherent in that practice, the collective (human) intelligence, brainstorming and the joy of reaching a useful, productive consensus cannot be replaced by A.I. within the coding cycle. Our products were always better when a team had some democratic involvement in the whole process; and, equally important, others in departments such as design and illustration, data analysis and production, would provide insights to such an extent that one could sometimes almost feel the contributions of all involved shining through the product itself at runtime.

I am neither convinced that A.I. can replace the human condition (as flawed as that is) and its important contribution to products that are mostly intended for people to use; or that A.I. cannot take a really impressive run at it.

A much more damning concern is those who really hold the cards. The Revenge of the Nerds period of the 70s, 80s and to a lesser extent the 90s, is largely over. But this is not for want of trying to immerse oneself in the joy of creativity, but simply because those who *do* hold the best (financial) hand today are those who are proudly such rabid money machinists.

Thank you for your time and insights. Your video is interesting and opens the debate on this topic.

What is needed now, though, is the debate ... globally and with strong cooperation.

Creativity and technology are very strong bedfellows. This is such an important part of what it means to be human that it is worth taking a strong resistive stance.

A.I. really could, and very much should, make all our lives better and more frictionless. What it must not be allowed to do is displace people ... people who need purpose, belonging and a common goal.

As long as Mr. and Mrs. $$$ call the shots - no matter that they will lead entire nations into universal darkness - we will never find genuine, lasting purpose and meaning again going forward.

If A.I. does manage to displace enough people, then there will be a terrible divide between wealthy maggots hiding behind <euphemism-alert> Mummy's apron <\euphemism-alert> and those who value their time and enjoy spending it making a genuinely creative contribution to the world.

The video correctly identifies that the current AI workflow is collaborative, requiring significant human input and review, and that "vibe coding" currently hits its limits on complex apps [03:14]. However, this is not a fundamental limitation of AI; it is an artifact of today's finite parameters and limited tokens.The video's claim that AI-generated code must be reviewed and refactored by a human to ensure it is "correct [and] maintainable" [05:05] is a classic misunderstanding of scaling laws in LLMs.The AI lacks the architectural wisdom to manage complexity, forcing the engineer to view the code itself as the value [05:52] and perform the high-level system design.

This perceived lack of architectural wisdom is simply a function of an insufficient parameter count.  Today's models operate in the 100-billion to trillion-parameter range. As future models scale to trillions of parameters, their ability to abstract, predict, and maintain large-scale system consistency will fundamentally exceed any single human architect. The 'complexity limit' the speaker hits is not a ceiling, but a checkpoint.  The fact is that the human's most efficient role is not to review lines of code, but to define the high-level system outcome and manage the AI's deployment pipeline.  The massive parameter count grants the AI Super-Refactoring capability, making human reorganization efforts obsolete and comparatively inefficient.

The video argues that raw code is the most efficient and "precise" way to understand system behavior [05:59], superior to any AI summary or explanation.
The AI can lose context or "misunderstand" a requirement in a complex prompt [06:26], forcing the engineer to read the code as the ultimate source of truth. This is why human coding skill is deemed indispensable [12:09]. The need for the human to read the code is a direct result of a constrained token context window. Today's models can only hold a fraction of a large codebase in their "working memory" at any given time. As context windows grow to millions of tokens, the AI will be able to ingest the entire codebase, all documentation, and the full history of interactions—creating a knowledge state that is inherently more precise and complete than the isolated human developer's understanding.In the future of true vibecoding, the human is the least efficient component for precision. The AI's internal token representation of the entire system will be the absolute source of truth. Trying to read thousands of lines of code to check the AI's work is a low-resolution bottleneck when the AI is capable of operating at the highest resolution of system knowledge.


Your conclusion that engineers must "learn AI and learn how to code" [12:34] is backward. It anchors the future of development in yesterday's inefficiencies.

commentText:
The "Wolt-ification" of AI is coming. When Wolt first launched, it was cheap AF. Everyone hyped it up because it felt like a steal, but they were just burning cash to get a "foot in the door." Once they became dominant, the prices spiked and people started abandoning the app.

We’re seeing the exact same play with AI orchestration, but with a much scarier "Physical Triangle" of costs:

The Electricity Bill: Running these models is a massive, growing drain on the power grid.

Hardware Demand: The price for GPUs, RAM, and chips is surging because physical supply can’t keep up.

The Complexity Gap: AI orchestration isn't just software; it's a massive, physical infrastructure expense.

This is an unequal triangle. The cost to run the "brain" is rising faster than the value it provides for basic tasks. Something has to give in 2026—either subscriptions triple in price, or companies stop using AI as the "main tool" for everything.

Remember: the bill always comes due—there’s no magic in the real world.

If you call yourself an “engineer” and don’t verify the work you put your name on, you are not an engineer, you are a programmer or a “prompt jockey.” An engineer, in any discipline, exists to take responsibility for outcomes, ensure proper processes are followed, and provide stakeholders with the confidence to make strategic decisions based on that work.

In my professional opinion, tools like these, like all tools before them, simply reinforce software engineering’s position as a core engineering discipline. The low-effort tasks these tools trivialise do not diminish the value I bring to projects. I have proven that over decades, even as new tools emerged claiming to make software engineers irrelevant. Typing commands is not the core of my function; it is something I can do and enjoy, but it is not why I am paid.

Many times in my career I have warned companies against cutting corners. I have also welcomed them back when they ignored that advice, made critical mistakes, and required an engineer to fix them. I have worked in this industry from the ground up, and for multiple companies I have taught why investing in entry-level engineers, upskilling them, and cultivating an engineering division is essential. Your engineering team is your core asset in a technology-driven world. You can outsource it or build it internally, but there is no shortcut.

I think of this in the same way we think about compilers. Before compilers existed, people had to write programs directly in assembly language. Even after compilers were introduced, there was a period when developers still needed to understand assembly to debug issues. I remember when I first started with Objective-C for iOS—I often had to dive into assembly to troubleshoot reference counting problems.

Over time, compilers became so powerful and efficient that most developers no longer think about assembly at all. I see LLMs following a similar trajectory. Right now, they don’t always produce production-ready code, and it still makes sense to understand the internals of programming languages. But as these models continue to improve, I believe we’ll reach a point where most developers won’t need deep knowledge of those internals anymore.

In a bubble, given infinite funding and time and source text, it's almost inevitable for LLMs to improve in how they perform at creating code that builds faster and more efficiently binaries. But there are problems in the premise there. First, nobody is saying that the next level of tools will cost the same. They are in the early times of charging less than what these tools cost or what they are worth, and that is due for a correction. It's early UBER days for LLMs. Second, training data is now scarce, and model collapse may be imminent. We have created 50 years of coding knowledge in the last 50 years, and it'll be another 10 until humans double it, but now much of that will be LLM written. Third, there could be legislative walls on natural/power resource usage and legislative walls on copyrights. Patents exist for human generated work, does an LLM generated codebase meet that standard? And it can reproduce open source licensed code because it was in the training data, but in projects that are the wrong license, and maybe courts will find a lot of projects in breach of GPL. Depends on how much money is on the table for those last three. And it's the entire economy at this point so it's the least worrying, but it exists.

That said, as it exists now, it is disrupting industry. It's not the real reason layoffs were happening, those were mostly economic in nature, things to do with pandemic staffing practices and interest rates. But we do have a talent glut, and people will be competing soon. In the world of tomorrow, everything will have wifi. Someone is building that code, and it will probably be one guy with a herd of LLMs per division for every product and company out there, so that's probably the future to work towards. ​@danielbennett5726 That analogy proves my point more than yours.

Autopilot didn’t eliminate pilots *yet*, but it drastically reduced workload and changed the job. And plenty of roles already disappeared because of tech - switchboard operators, typists, video rental clerks, travel agents, toll booth collectors, elevator operators, human computers, photo lab developers, typesetters, bowling alley pinsetters...

The real pattern isn’t “AI replaces 100% overnight,” it’s:
less humans needed -> roles shrink -> eventually some disappear.

AI doesn’t need to be perfect - just better than humans on average. And that bar isn’t as high as people think.

Even if AI replaces “only” half of developers, that’s still massive. Fewer roles, more competition, and the job itself shifts from building to supervising.

At that point, it’s not even the same profession people originally got into, which is solving problems by writing code.

title: AI Was Supposed to Replace Developers... Until It Couldn't
commentText: I started a project as a test back in the summer with no prior knowledge/experience of coding with AI. Lots of amazing realizations, and also some serious challenges.  However, as I became more familiar, in 6 months I was able to bring an app to alpha, in python, typescript and deploy it on a droplet, none of which I have ever used in my professional career.  Because I know and understand system architecture, I was able to get AI to do what I wanted, but that also was a process of creating my commands and guardrails.  I am also paying for a $200 month subscription in order to process all my requests.  The flip side, by AI's estimations, I did in about 1000 hours what would have taken a team of 3 (senior developer and 2 competent coders) appox 2.5 years.  So I would say the acceleration  rate in my experience is somewere between 12:1 andd 18:1 based on the analysis both myself and the AI have done in human hours.   Yes you can get it to do some jobs autonomously, but the less you are engaged with what AI is doing in each process, the more likely you are going to end up with a mess and iterating over the bad code to either remove or fix it.  Also I can confirm that AI is EXTEMELY good with db/backend.  This process went so fast it literally blew my mind.  Where it struggles is with frontend development, and things slow down a bit.  Unit and Mock testing is also very fast and again I was quite impressed.   My takeaway from this video is the overall analysis as to where and how AI fits in is very accurate and I have over 1000 hours in.  As for languages I am familiar with, or projects I have coded myself, it's an invaluable tool for debugging and optimizing.  But again, you have to understand architecture, all the actors involved and where your separations of concerns lie.  AI likes to make assumptions about what you are doing and thats where it gets you in trouble.

commentText:
There has to be a skilled developer in the loop when working with agents, otherwise you won't catch the moment where the AI goes slightly off the path you intend, and you end up with a solution that is hard to maintain, or contains bugs or vulnerabilities, it is not appropriate for the problem at hand.

Sure agents can be a productivity booster if done correctly, but it doesn't totally replace software engineers all together, and you still have to be good at managing context, tell it the right intentions, and catch it if it's doing a bad job.
Also if you start using AI to your advantage in your company, you might have a slight advantage over other companies who's not currently using AI. But when the other companies start using AI as well your company doesn't have an advantage any longer, and then you need more software engineers to keep up, cause the "software engineers with AI" is the new normal.
There's been countless of tools introduced throughout time. Computers, internet, Microsoft Teams, Excel, Word, Outlook. They all change how we work. And people work more efficient, but all these things is the new normal now, and every worker is using them. I think the same thing will happen with AI.
People were also afraid that computers would replace them back when they were introduced, but you still need the person operating the computer.

My advice as a mid-to-high level software engineer, is to try to not be stressed about AI. It's a relatively new technology. Tools are evolving crazy fast, it's hard to keep up with the newest developments. But EVERYONE feels the same way: "Oh sh*t, is everyone besides me doing AI right now!? Am I going extinct?! What about all my skills and education?!" 

Don't worry. Keep an eye on AI. Try it out, see if it can do just one repetitive task you used to do, or help you in some way. Then you learn how to use it, you see more ways to use it gradually. And tools will only become better and easy to work with as time passes.

AI is not perfect. It's like a wild horse that you need to steer and keep on the path of intentions. If you let it run free, you'll end up in the forrest, and you'll have to spend a lot of time getting back to the path. But if you can steer it left or right and keep it on the path, you might be slightly faster than the seasoned runner, who does things efficiently and manually himself.
We're used to running, and doing things efficiently by ourselves, but now we need to learn to ride horses, and we don't learn that in 1 day. But eventually everyone's gonna ride horses, and it'll be easy, and the new normal. But don't stress about not knowing how to ride horses yet - don't stress about not knowing how to use agents efficiently yet. But try tinker with it, and keep an eye on it. And learn from your coworkers.

AI has not replaced developers; it has raised the bar for understanding, design, and long‑term thinking while making shallow, copy‑paste learning paths much less viable.
​

What actually caused the pain
The 2023–24 “AI panic” got blamed for layoffs, but most cuts came from over‑hiring, rising rates, and companies correcting after the 2020–22 boom, not from AI eliminating all dev work.
​

AI hype made many beginners think “learning to code” meant just prompting tools instead of building solid skills, which backfired once hiring got tighter.
​

How AI really changed dev work
AI now writes a big chunk of routine code, so value shifted from typing solutions to understanding architectures, trade‑offs, and how to make systems scale and survive in production.
​

Senior‑style thinking (debugging, design, edge cases, maintainability) became important much earlier in a dev’s journey, even for juniors.
​

The new risks for learners
The main danger is shallow understanding: shipping code you don’t really understand, over‑relying on AI, and never building the mental models needed to solve harder problems later.
​

The “easy path” of tutorials plus copy‑pasted AI answers might get you simple projects done but leaves you stuck when something breaks off the happy path.
​

Are junior jobs gone?
Junior roles are fewer and expectations are higher, but companies still need developers who can think, debug, and collaborate, not just prompt models.
​

Those who combine basics (HTML/CSS/JS, core backend concepts, debugging) with smart AI usage and real projects still have a path in.
​

What “learning properly” means now
You need consistent, hands‑on practice: building projects from scratch, breaking things, fixing them, and only then using AI as a helper instead of a crutch.
​

The winners in this new era are thoughtful engineers who understand why code works, can reason about systems, and use AI to go deeper—not to avoid thinking.

title: AI Was Supposed to Replace Developers. Here’s What Actually Happened.
commentText: While the video rightly pushes back against exaggerated claims that AI would instantly replace developers, it arguably downplays deeper structural changes in the industry. Productivity gains from AI may not eliminate engineers outright, but they can still reduce demand by allowing smaller teams to do the same work, which affects hiring, especially for juniors. The argument also assumes AI’s current limits will hold, even though its capabilities have been advancing rapidly, particularly in system reasoning and code generation. In addition, suggesting that the solution is simply “learn fundamentals better” overlooks the real issue that many traditional training pathways — like learning through repetitive junior work — are disappearing. Finally, framing AI mainly as a helpful productivity tool risks ignoring how employers may use those productivity gains to increase expectations, compress salaries, or reduce team sizes, meaning the impact on the profession could be more gradual but still significant.

​​​@Developete A good analogy, I think, is teaching. Teachers don't simply give students the answers because they understand learning happens from thinking about the problem and trying things that don't work until a solution is found. That's why we're rewarded with a thrilling "ah hah! moment" when we do it that way: it's _good for us_ . When a LLM simply tells us the problem we're short-circuiting that entire process, so that we can get on with stuff we already know how to do. Growth comes from _resistance_ , not from ease.

For the most part I don't use AI at all when coding. Not even auto-complete. I type all the characters by hand; I look up function definitions in documentation when necessary (though that isn't often, because I remember them, because I haven't lost the ability to remember them from relying on auto-complete), which means sometimes finding even more appropriate functions by happenstance, or noticing functions which turn out useful later; I think deeply about how to solve tasks; and on the rare occasions I create a bug I fix it the old fashioned way, by thinking about it and applying a process of elimination. Auto-complete popups are imo distracting and focus-breaking in the same way as phone notifications.

This means I code more slowly than the modern average, but it also means my _intuition_ has the opportunity to kick in. I'll often write code a certain way, then get an intuitive sense there's a different approach which is better—and sometimes that can lead to discovering an entirely better _pattern_ or _structure_ for a significant part of the system. I'm _immersed_ in the code, allowing my entire mind to operate on it, not merely my fast-decision, instinctive, rational mind. IMO it results in higher quality code which I fully understand, a much greater sense of satisfaction, and much higher rates of learning because I'm more often _pushing against resistance_ rather than simply coasting. In my view all these automated tools put devs into a kind of _manic_ frame of mind, and that's not a good place from which to produce high-quality work.

I've been doing this for 40 years and there's much more I could say about the ruthless and uncompromising pursuit of excellence, and the importance of process over product and of _slowing the f— down_ , but watching some interviews with Ginger Bill (inventor of the Odin language) might be useful: he's nearly as stubborn/old-school about things like auto-complete ;)

(BTW, I think the shift to emphasizing _rushing_ , aka "productivity," over _thoughtfulness, care, and deep understanding_ is the reason so few devs these days can code well in dynamic languages, must rely on a compiler to catch basic errors, and have rationalized this by declaring statically typed languages intrinsically superior. It's untrue and a great shame, imo, but fashion is as fashion does. It's also the reason so much modern software frankly sucks.)

commentText:
Programming and software is entirely mechanical so it better be done by mechanical devices and not a human. Anybody that thinks that they are smarter than AI and will control it is gaslighting others and will be humbled. Dave Farley’s argument in this video rests on a fundamentally static view of what AI is and what software engineering will become. His core premise is that AI is merely a "fast typist" that accelerates code generation—which was never the bottleneck and thereby creates a "complexity bomb" unless rigidly restrained by Continuous Delivery (CD) and test-driven human oversight.

Farley argues that the bottleneck in software was never typing, but rather "understanding, designing, testing, and integrating."

This deliberately undersells what current and near-future models actually do. AI is not simply generating syntax; it is raising the fundamental level of abstraction. By offloading the implementation details—memory management, boilerplate, API scaffolding—the human cognitive bandwidth is freed entirely for the systems architecture and design that Farley rightly prizes. Furthermore, advanced models are  capable of structural reasoning, meaning they are assisting in the "designing and integrating" phases, not the typing.

Farley invokes Jevons Paradox (making code cheaper means we produce more of it, increasing the maintenance burden and complexity).

Jevons Paradox assumes the cost of the remedy remains static while consumption grows. But AI doesn't just lower the cost of writing code; it exponentially lowers the cost of reading, refactoring, and maintaining it. If an AI can generate a million lines of code, an AI agent can also parse, audit, and trace execution paths through a million lines of code in seconds. The maintenance burden doesn't scale linearly with human effort anymore because the AI itself absorbs the overhead of managing the complexity it created.

Farley claims AI cannot judge context or understand the broader scope of what a system is trying to achieve (e.g., security risks, user volume, business logic).

This is a snapshot of legacy LLM limitations, not a fundamental barrier. With context windows now scaling into the millions of tokens, models can ingest entire code repositories, architecture diagrams, pull request histories, and business requirement documents simultaneously. A model holding the entire state of a monolithic architecture in its active context actually possesses more immediate systemic context than a human developer, who typically only works on an isolated microservice or feature branch.

Farley argues good engineering requires small, reversible steps (TDD, CI/CD) and that AI inherently makes dangerous "giant leaps."

The tendency for AI to make "giant leaps" is an artifact of chat-based user interfaces, not the models themselves. In an agentic workflow, an AI does not need to output a massive block of code and pray that it works. Autonomous coding agents are specifically designed to operate in iterative loops—writing a failing test, writing the implementation, reading the compiler error, and adjusting. AI is actually perfectly suited to the hyper-disciplined, micro-step methodology Farley advocates; it just executes those loops at machine speed.

Farley concludes that AI won't replace software engineering, but rather expose teams that weren't doing real engineering.

This relies on shifting the goalposts of what "replacement" means. If AI handles 90% of the cognitive labor of implementation, writes its own tests, and validates against an automated deployment pipeline, the traditional role of the software engineer has been replaced. The human evolves from a "creator of software" into a "director of agents" and an allocator of compute. To say the profession hasn't been replaced because someone still needs to prompt the business requirements is like saying the profession of a factory weaver wasn't replaced by the power loom because someone still had to switch the machine on.

I think “AI won’t replace software engineering” is true, but maybe not because AI is only a coding tool.

The deeper issue is that software engineering is not just code production. It is context, judgment, tradeoffs, history, responsibility, and knowing which “correct” fix is dangerous in the real system.

When AI fails at coding, people often focus on the bad output.

But the more interesting question is:

“What was missing from the situation that made this bad output possible?”

A human engineer does not work from code alone. They carry architecture, production experience, team conventions, past failures, and invisible constraints. Much of engineering skill is not in typing the code, but in knowing what the code means inside a living system.

So maybe the future question is not whether AI can write code.

It is whether our systems are understandable enough for any intelligence, human or artificial, to safely act on them.

That is where I think the debate gets interesting.

Increasingly, the AI understands the domain space well, particularly after discussions and feed back on small feature-specific wireframes or prototypes. Increasingly, I spend the majority of my time thinking about hard problems and then talking them through with the agent until that is rigorously described. @AndrewEddie AI success depends on the programming language and the task complexity. It also depends on the prompt constraints. Naturally, if the task is very small, about 300 lines of code, and the context is properly limited, the AI knows where to get all the necessary info. My business process looks the same as yours. Otherwise, I would just delete everything the AI did. You need to provide a detailed plan, specific constraints, and a small task. Only then is there something useful in the output. It usually still requires fixes, but using AI pays off.

commentText:
This is an absolutely misleading example regarding radiology and a textbook lie. Jensen ignores hard data about the global workforce: roughly 60% of employees bring no added value, and another 15% actively act against the company, creating losses. These 75% are essentially redundant. AI will not merely 'change their tools'; AI will simply filter them out and replace them.

Furthermore, regarding radiologists, he is comparing apples to oranges. The AI he mentions in relation to 2020 was narrowly specialized computer vision. It could find a tumor, but it couldn't establish a complex diagnosis or write a medical report. Human intervention was necessary both factually and legally.

However, with today's LLM assistants, even that factual necessity has fallen away. AI can now handle data synthesis, context, and report writing. The only thing genuinely left for the human is legal liability. A radiologist today essentially functions like a COO—formally adding a signature to a decision and bearing responsibility for it, but almost all the actual work has already been done by something else. Comparing this narrow, legally protected top-tier group to the general workforce, where no such safeguard exists, is a total illusion. The vast majority will be replaced, and very quickly.

References:

Gallup - State of the Global Workplace Reports: Consistent data on 15% of employees being "actively disengaged" (working against the firm) and ~60% "not engaged" (adding no special value).

The Vitality Curve (Jack Welch/GE): The established "20-70-10" rule identifying the bottom 10% as underperformers causing net losses.

Price’s Law: A common statistical model in organizations showing that 50% of work is produced by the square root of the total number of employees (meaning the vast majority contribute minimal value).

I am a systems engineer with 25 years of experience. I’ve always resented the need to learn code to be effective in my role. I do have a good knowledge of PowerShell and SQL and have a solid understanding of object-oriented programming, but it still feels like pulling teeth to sit down and work line by line to create, update, or fix code.

I spent eight years as an application support engineer, working in SQL every day. Even then, anything beyond updating a report or comparing a few tables felt onerous—because writing code and doing support are fundamentally different kinds of work. My focus was always on the next ticket or making tools to help resolve the next ticket, not on deepening my familiarity with a new library or refining my coding skills.

Since the rise of AI, I’ve started shifting into a more design-centered approach to get the most out of it, and that’s been essential. More than anything else, that shift has pulled me back into learning code—but from a different angle. By asking critical questions about why something works the way it does, AI helps surface the missing pieces that connect the dots.

Design is engaging. It provides context and intent. Coding, on its own, still isn’t something I naturally gravitate toward—but when it’s driven by design, it finally feels purposeful.

commentText:
​@fwdflashwebdesign  Your argument rests on a romantic, yet fundamentally flawed, premise: that a human signature is a guarantee of accuracy or quality.

It isn't. A human signature is merely a mechanism of liability.

When you pay for a certified translation and a human stamps it, that stamp does not magically bend reality to ensure the translation is perfectly nuanced and free of errors. Human translators get tired, miss context, and make catastrophic errors all the time. The signature simply tells you who to sue or fire when things go wrong. It is an insurance policy, not a proof of mathematical correctness.

You say we "can't trust AI no matter how good it is," but we already implicitly trust automated systems over human verification in environments far more complex than document translation.

Think about modern software architecture. When you design a full-stack application, perhaps using a Python backend to scrape and process massive amounts of data, storing it in an SQLite database, and dynamically serving it to a React frontend, you do not have a human "sign off" on every data transfer. You don't trust a human to manually verify the memory safety of a complex system; you trust the strict, automated rules of the Rust compiler. We trust the machine because machines are highly consistent, while humans are consistently erratic.

The anxiety around AI is that it is a probabilistic engine (it hallucinates, it guesses). This is true. But the solution isn't to regress to a guy with a pen stamping a piece of paper. The solution is deterministic verification.

If an AI translates a legal contract, the future of verification isn't a human reading it. The future is an automated pipeline where:
LLM Agent A translates the document.
LLM Agent B (trained strictly on legal adversarial logic) critiques the translation for loopholes.
A deterministic, non-AI script checks the output against a hardcoded dictionary of mandatory legal terms.
That pipeline is infinitely more rigorous, auditable, and trustworthy than a single human expert who had a bad cup of coffee that morning.

Trust in the 20th century was built on human credentials (degrees, stamps, signatures). Trust in the 21st century is built on cryptography, automated testing, and CI/CD pipelines.

If an AI generates a complex block of code, you don't trust it because it looks pretty. You trust it because you run it through a rigorous suite of automated unit tests, and the tests pass green. The passing test suite is the new signature. The AI is the laborer; the deterministic test is the notary.

We are in a transitional phase where society still demands the comforting theater of a human signature, simply because we haven't fully standardized the legal frameworks for algorithmic liability yet. But make no mistake: we are preserving the human in the loop for our own psychological comfort, not for superior accuracy.

Charles Petzold’s "Code" and the Nand2Tetris project teach the one principle that every digital system—past, present, and future—must respect:

Electrons → Transistors → Binary Logic → The Stack → Software.

AI, quantum processors, and future tech still must communicate with a world built on this foundation. Until someone reinvents computing beneath the level of the electron and the logic gate, every "revolution" will still run through this stack—and require someone who understands it.

That’s why engineers who know the full stack—not just how to use AI, but how AI runs on silicon—can never be fully automated or replaced.

They aren't just tool-users; they're tool-understanders.
And you can't replace the person who knows why the tool works.

I usually turn off the AI suggestions unless I have it in a clear context when it will make sense and I feel lazy. Otherwise it makes up variables, file names, functions, as if from some bits of code it saw randomly on Stack Overflow. It sometimes blunders ahead with nonsense, breaking my concentration.

It's like a toddler offering to help you by scribbling on your work with their crayons. Occasionally a precocious toddler, but a toddler none the less.

Recently working on an IPYNB file, the Copilot agent also deleted all the cells after the row it was 'fixing.' Half the code was gone. When I pointed that out, it apologized profusely. Like that did a lot to fix its mistake. 

Fortunately I was able to restore the cells from a prior checkpoint. I then banned the agent from making code changes -- it could only offer suggestions in the chat window that I could copy and paste (or not). It actually wrote a little contract to that effect at the end of the notebook.

Which, of course, it then ignored.
